newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Issing sees Germany joining EMU on time.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Issing sees Germany joining EMU on time.

text.p: Weighing into the debate on which nations will be able to join Europe's planned currency union at the end of the decade, a senior Bundesbank offical said Germany can still make the date, if it works very hard.

"It will be difficult for Germany to meet EMU deficits but it is still possible," Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing told journalists on Friday at a conference on international monetary policy outside of Frankfurt.

While Germany's six top economics institutes earlier this week predicted Germany's 1997 budget deficit will likely be 3.5 percent, far exceeding the reference value of three percent, Issing called the forecast "premature".
To join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) nations must show their inflation rates are low, currencies are stable and deficits are at low levels.
The Maastricht Treaty on EMU puts the reference values for nations' planned or actual government deficit and debt to gross domestic product as three percent and 60 percent, respectively.
Political leaders will decide early in 1998 which nations can join EMU after reviewing their 1997 economic data.
Asked to comment on France's plan to whip its finances into shape by including a transfer of funds from France Telecom, Issing said such a step muddled the issue.

"This kind of precedent leads to a lack of clarity. The main factor in public finances is sustainability," Issing said after the European Commission this week ruled to allow France to include the transfer.
Separately, in a speech, Issing warned that despite signs to the contrary, inflationary dangers have not been permanently defeated yet.

"The danger of inflation is not dead simply because current statistics testify to price stability," Issing said, adding he did not want to join a growing chorus of economists who are declaring that inflation has been conquered.
Looking ahead Issing said "the fight against inflation will not have been won definitely until inflation has disappeared once and for all from the range of policy options."

To root out inflationary dangers, central banks must be independent, solely committed to price stability and be able to "put this goal into practice by credibly applying their set of instruments," Issing said.
Issing warned that in light of alarmingly high debt levels in some countries, "this will be the only way to prevent renewed considertaion being given to inflation tax."

In Germany most independent economists forecast inflation rates, which stood at at 1.5 percent in West Germany during October, will rise slightly in the coming months. However, they do not believe this is cause for concern.
